about: Thermodynamics 1 (MECH40003) is a core 5-credit Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Mechanical Engineering. The 2026-27 programme specification lists it as running from the Autumn to the Summer term. A third-party University of California study-abroad listing (last reviewed 2021-22) describes it as introducing the fundamental laws of thermodynamics and applying them to simple engineering problems, at a pace suited to students meeting the subject for the first time. Imperial's detailed module descriptor could not be opened for this pack, so the topics follow a standard first course built from that description: basic concepts, the first law for closed and flow processes, properties of substances, the second law and entropy, and an introduction to power cycles. No module-specific assessment breakdown was found; the programme specification gives only a Year 1 average of roughly 75% examination. Steam property values here are approximate (from IAPWS-IF97), so use your department's data book in exams.
topics: Energy, heat, work and the first law
Consequences of the second law: entropy

notes.h: Systems, properties, state and the ideal gas
notes.body:
Thermodynamics is about energy and how it changes form. Before using any law you must say exactly what you are analysing, and most marks lost in first-year papers come from a badly defined system or mixed-up units.

Systems
- A closed system (a control mass) has a fixed mass. Energy can cross its boundary as heat or work, but matter cannot. Example: gas trapped in a piston–cylinder.
- An open system (a control volume) has mass flowing across its boundary. Examples: a turbine, a pump, a nozzle.
- An isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy with its surroundings.
- The boundary can be real or imaginary, fixed or moving. Draw it on your sketch every time.

Properties and state
- A property is any measurable characteristic of the system at a given state: pressure p, temperature T, volume V, mass m, internal energy U and so on.
- Extensive properties scale with the amount of matter (V, U, m). Intensive properties do not (p, T, density).
- Dividing an extensive property by mass gives a specific property, written in lower case: v = V/m, u = U/m, h = H/m.
- The state postulate: the state of a simple compressible pure substance is fixed by two independent intensive properties. Note that p and T are not independent during a phase change.

Equilibrium and processes
- A system is in equilibrium when its properties are uniform and do not change unless something outside changes.
- A process is a change from one equilibrium state to another. A quasi-static (quasi-equilibrium) process happens slowly enough that the system passes through equilibrium states, so it can be drawn as a line on a p–V diagram.
- A cycle returns the system to its starting state, so the net change of every property over a cycle is zero.

Temperature and pressure
- The zeroth law: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is what makes a thermometer meaningful.
- Always use kelvin in thermodynamic equations: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
- Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa = 100 kPa; standard atmosphere = 1.01325 bar.

The ideal gas
- pV = mRT, or pv = RT, where R is the specific gas constant: R = R̄/M with R̄ = 8.314 kJ/(kmol K).
- For air, M ≈ 28.97 kg/kmol, so R ≈ 0.287 kJ/(kg K).
- The model works well at low pressure and at temperatures well above the critical temperature.

Worked example: a 0.5 m³ rigid tank holds air at 5 bar and 27 °C. Then m = pV/(RT) = (5 × 10⁵ × 0.5)/(287 × 300.15) ≈ 2.90 kg. If you use pressure in pascals, R must be in J/(kg K). If you use kPa, R must be in kJ/(kg K).

Exam tips: define the system and its boundary first, convert to kelvin and absolute pressure straight away, and keep the units of R consistent with the units of pressure.

notes.h: Work, heat and the first law for closed systems
notes.body:
Energy crosses the boundary of a closed system in only two ways: as work or as heat. Both are path functions. Their values depend on how the process is carried out, not just on the end states, so we write δW and δQ for small amounts rather than dW and dQ.

Sign convention
- In this note, Q is heat added to the system and W is work done by the system. The first law for a closed system is then Q − W = ΔU (+ ΔKE + ΔPE if the system moves).
- Some UK textbooks and lecture courses count work done on the system as positive, which turns the law into Q + W = ΔU. Use whichever convention your lecture notes use, state it, and stick to it.

Boundary (displacement) work
- For a quasi-static process, W = ∫ p dV, which is the area under the path on a p–V diagram.
- Constant volume: W = 0.
- Constant pressure: W = p(V₂ − V₁).
- Polytropic process pVⁿ = constant (n ≠ 1): W = (p₂V₂ − p₁V₁)/(1 − n). For an ideal gas this equals mR(T₂ − T₁)/(1 − n).
- Isothermal ideal gas (n = 1): W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁).
- Other kinds of work include shaft work, paddle-wheel (stirring) work and electrical work. Stirring work can only be done on a system, never extracted from it.

Internal energy and enthalpy
- U is a property, so ΔU depends only on the end states. Enthalpy is defined as H = U + pV, and h = u + pv per unit mass.
- For an ideal gas, u and h depend only on temperature: Δu = c_v ΔT and Δh = c_p ΔT (constant specific heats). Also c_p − c_v = R and γ = c_p/c_v. For air, c_p ≈ 1.005 kJ/(kg K), c_v ≈ 0.718 kJ/(kg K) and γ ≈ 1.4.
- In a constant-pressure quasi-static process in a closed system with only boundary work (no shaft, stirring or electrical work), Q = ΔH.

First law for a cycle
- Over a cycle ΔU = 0, so the net heat in equals the net work out: ∮δQ = ∮δW.

Worked example: 1 kg of air at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed quasi-statically with pV¹·³ = constant to 8 bar.
- Polytropic temperature relation: T₂ = T₁(p₂/p₁)^((n−1)/n) = 300 × 8^(0.3/1.3) ≈ 484.8 K.
- Work done by the air: W = mR(T₂ − T₁)/(1 − n) = 0.287 × 184.8/(−0.3) ≈ −176.8 kJ. The minus sign means 176.8 kJ of work is done on the air.
- ΔU = m c_v (T₂ − T₁) = 0.718 × 184.8 ≈ 132.7 kJ.
- Q = ΔU + W = 132.7 − 176.8 ≈ −44.1 kJ, so about 44 kJ of heat is rejected during the compression.

Exam tips: sketch the p–V diagram, write the first law with a stated sign convention, and look up or calculate ΔU separately from W. Never assume Q = 0 unless the question says the process is adiabatic.

notes.h: Pure substances, phase change and property tables
notes.body:
Steam is the classic working fluid of mechanical engineering, and it does not behave as an ideal gas near saturation. You must be able to work out the phase of a state and read property tables quickly and correctly.

Phases and saturation
- At a given pressure, a pure substance boils at the saturation temperature Tsat(p). At a given temperature, it boils at the saturation pressure psat(T).
- A compressed (subcooled) liquid has T < Tsat at its pressure. A saturated liquid (subscript f) is just about to boil. A saturated vapour (subscript g) is just about to condense. A superheated vapour has T > Tsat.
- On a T–v diagram the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour lines meet at the critical point. For water this is about 374 °C and 220.6 bar. Above the critical point there is no distinct boiling.
- The triple point of water is 0.01 °C at about 0.0061 bar (611.7 Pa).

Wet steam and quality
- In the two-phase region, the dryness fraction (quality) is x = mass of vapour ÷ total mass, with 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.
- Any specific property y (v, u, h, s) is y = y_f + x(y_g − y_f) = y_f + x y_fg.
- Rearranging gives x = (y − y_f)/y_fg. Use whichever property you are given.

Using the tables
- Saturation tables list Tsat, v_f, v_g, h_f, h_fg, h_g, s_f, s_g and so on against pressure (or temperature).
- Superheat tables give v, u, h and s at each (p, T) pair. Interpolate linearly between rows.
- For a compressed liquid at modest pressure, use the saturated-liquid values at the same temperature: v ≈ v_f(T), u ≈ u_f(T), h ≈ h_f(T).
- To find the phase from (p, T): compare T with Tsat(p). From (p, v) or (p, h): compare with the f and g values at that pressure.

Approximate values (IAPWS-IF97; your data book may differ slightly in the last figure)
- 0.1 bar: Tsat ≈ 45.8 °C, h_f ≈ 191.8, h_fg ≈ 2392.1, h_g ≈ 2583.9 kJ/kg; s_f ≈ 0.649, s_g ≈ 8.149 kJ/(kg K).
- 1 bar: Tsat ≈ 99.6 °C, h_f ≈ 417.5, h_fg ≈ 2257.5, h_g ≈ 2675.0 kJ/kg; v_g ≈ 1.694 m³/kg.
- 10 bar: Tsat ≈ 179.9 °C, h_f ≈ 762.5, h_fg ≈ 2014.6, h_g ≈ 2777.1 kJ/kg; v_g ≈ 0.1944 m³/kg.
- Superheated, 40 bar and 400 °C: v ≈ 0.0734 m³/kg, h ≈ 3214.4 kJ/kg, s ≈ 6.771 kJ/(kg K).

Worked example: wet steam at 10 bar with x = 0.9.
- T = Tsat ≈ 179.9 °C.
- h = 762.5 + 0.9 × 2014.6 ≈ 2575.6 kJ/kg.
- v ≈ v_f + x(v_g − v_f) ≈ 0.0011 + 0.9 × (0.1944 − 0.0011) ≈ 0.175 m³/kg. Because v_f is tiny, x v_g is a good approximation.

Ideal-gas limit
- Steam at low pressure and high superheat behaves nearly as an ideal gas. Near the saturation line it does not, so use the tables there.

Exam tips: always decide the phase first, write the formula y = y_f + x y_fg before substituting, and quote which table row you used. Interpolation errors are a common way to lose marks.

notes.h: Steady-flow energy equation and engineering devices
notes.body:
Most real machines are open systems with fluid flowing through them. The first law for a control volume adds two ideas to the closed-system version: conservation of mass, and the energy carried in and out by the flowing fluid.

Mass conservation
- For steady flow, ṁ = ρAV is the same at inlet and outlet: ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂, or A₁V₁/v₁ = A₂V₂/v₂.

Flow work and enthalpy
- Pushing fluid into a control volume takes work pv per unit mass. Combining this with internal energy gives the enthalpy, h = u + pv. This is why enthalpy, not internal energy, appears in the flow equation.

The steady-flow energy equation (SFEE)
- With Q̇ as heat added and Ẇ as shaft power produced: Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (V₂² − V₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)].
- Units trap: h is usually in kJ/kg while V²/2 comes out in J/kg. Divide the kinetic-energy term by 1000 before adding.

Standard devices (usual assumptions)
- Turbine: adiabatic, ΔKE and ΔPE negligible, so w = h₁ − h₂.
- Compressor or pump: w_in = h₂ − h₁. For an incompressible liquid in a reversible pump, w_in ≈ v(p₂ − p₁).
- Nozzle: no work and adiabatic, so V₂ = √(V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂)), with h in J/kg. A diffuser is the reverse.
- Throttling valve: no work, adiabatic, negligible ΔKE, so h₂ = h₁. Pressure falls. For an ideal gas the temperature stays the same; for steam or a refrigerant it usually falls.
- Boiler, condenser or heat exchanger: no work, so Q̇ = ṁ(h₂ − h₁) for each stream.
- Mixing chamber: Σṁh in = Σṁh out when adiabatic.

Worked example 1 (turbine): steam enters at 30 bar and 350 °C (h ≈ 3116.1 kJ/kg) and leaves at 0.1 bar with x = 0.9.
- h₂ = 191.8 + 0.9 × 2392.1 ≈ 2344.7 kJ/kg.
- w = 3116.1 − 2344.7 ≈ 771.4 kJ/kg. At 10 kg/s the power is about 7.71 MW.

Worked example 2 (throttling calorimeter): wet steam at 10 bar is throttled to 1 bar and leaves at 120 °C (h ≈ 2716.6 kJ/kg).
- Since h is constant, 2716.6 = 762.5 + x × 2014.6, giving x ≈ 0.970.
- This is a classic way of measuring the dryness of nearly dry steam.

Worked example 3 (air nozzle): air with negligible inlet velocity cools from 500 K to 440 K adiabatically. Then V₂ = √(2 × 1005 × 60) ≈ 347 m/s.

Unsteady problems such as filling a tank use the same ideas, but the stored energy changes with time. Treat them separately and only if they are on your syllabus.

Exam tips: state every assumption (steady, adiabatic, ΔKE ≈ 0, and so on), write the full SFEE first and then cross out terms, and watch the kJ versus J trap in the kinetic-energy term.

notes.h: Heat engines, reversibility and the Carnot limit
notes.body:
The first law says energy is conserved, but it does not say which way processes go or how much heat can be turned into work. The second law answers both questions.

Heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps
- A heat engine takes heat Q_H from a hot reservoir, produces net work W and rejects Q_L to a cold reservoir. Over a cycle, W = Q_H − Q_L, and the thermal efficiency is η = W/Q_H = 1 − Q_L/Q_H.
- A refrigerator uses work to move heat Q_L out of a cold space: COP_R = Q_L/W.
- A heat pump delivers Q_H to a warm space: COP_HP = Q_H/W = COP_R + 1.
- A thermal reservoir is a body so large that its temperature does not change when heat is added or removed.

Two statements of the second law
- Kelvin–Planck: no device working in a cycle can receive heat from a single reservoir and produce an equal amount of work. Every heat engine must reject some heat, so η < 100%.
- Clausius: no device working in a cycle can have, as its only effect, the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter one. A refrigerator needs work input.
- The two statements are equivalent: a device that broke one could be combined with an ordinary machine to break the other.

Reversible and irreversible processes
- A reversible process can be undone, leaving no change in either the system or its surroundings. It is an idealisation.
- Sources of irreversibility include friction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, unrestrained (free) expansion, mixing of different fluids, and electrical resistance.

The Carnot cycle and Carnot principles
- The Carnot cycle has two reversible isothermal heat transfers and two reversible adiabatic (isentropic) processes.
- Carnot principles: (1) no engine between two given reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible one; (2) all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, whatever the working fluid.
- This leads to the thermodynamic (Kelvin) temperature scale, with Q_H/Q_L = T_H/T_L for a reversible cycle.

Limits (temperatures in kelvin)
- η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H.
- COP_R,max = T_L/(T_H − T_L).
- COP_HP,max = T_H/(T_H − T_L).

Worked example: an inventor claims an engine that takes 600 kW from a source at 800 K, rejects heat at 300 K and produces 400 kW.
- The claimed efficiency is 400/600 ≈ 66.7%.
- The Carnot limit is 1 − 300/800 = 62.5%.
- The claim exceeds the limit, so it breaks the second law and is impossible.

Worked example: the best possible heat pump keeping a house at 20 °C when it is 0 °C outside has COP_HP = 293.15/20 ≈ 14.7. Real heat pumps achieve far less because of irreversibility and finite temperature differences in their heat exchangers.

Exam tips: convert every temperature to kelvin before using a Carnot expression, say which statement of the second law you are using, and when judging a claim compare it with the reversible limit.

The second law gives us a new property, entropy, which lets us measure irreversibility and set a standard for real machines.

The Clausius inequality and entropy
- For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality only for a reversible cycle.
- This means δQ_rev/T integrates to the same value along every reversible path, so it defines a property: dS = δQ_rev/T.
- For any process, S₂ − S₁ = ∫δQ/T + S_gen, where S_gen ≥ 0 is the entropy generated by irreversibility. S_gen = 0 only for a reversible process.
- For an isolated system, ΔS ≥ 0. This is the increase-of-entropy principle.

The T ds relations
- T ds = du + p dv and T ds = dh − v dp. They link entropy to measurable properties and hold for any process between equilibrium states, because they relate properties only.

Entropy changes
- Ideal gas with constant specific heats: s₂ − s₁ = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁).
- Incompressible solid or liquid: s₂ − s₁ = c ln(T₂/T₁).
- Steam: read s from the tables, using s = s_f + x s_fg for wet states.
- A thermal reservoir receiving heat Q at temperature T: ΔS = Q/T.

Isentropic processes
- A process that is adiabatic and reversible is isentropic (s constant). For an ideal gas with constant specific heats this gives pv^γ = constant and T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ).
- On a T–s diagram, the area under a reversible path is the heat transferred. Isentropic processes are vertical lines.

Isentropic efficiencies
- Turbine: η_T = actual work ÷ isentropic work = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s).
- Compressor or pump: η_C = isentropic work ÷ actual work = (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁).
- Both are compared with the isentropic process between the same inlet state and the same exit pressure.

Worked example (compressor): air at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed adiabatically to 8 bar with η_C = 0.85 (c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg K), γ = 1.4).
- T₂s = 300 × 8^(0.4/1.4) ≈ 543.4 K.
- T₂ = 300 + (543.4 − 300)/0.85 ≈ 586.4 K.
- Actual work = 1.005 × 286.4 ≈ 287.8 kJ/kg. The isentropic work would be about 244.7 kJ/kg.
- Entropy rise = 1.005 ln(586.4/300) − 0.287 ln 8 ≈ 0.077 kJ/(kg K). This is positive, as it must be for an adiabatic irreversible process.

Worked example (heat transfer): 1000 kJ flows from a reservoir at 500 K to one at 300 K.
- S_gen = 1000/300 − 1000/500 ≈ 1.33 kJ/K. The finite temperature difference is a source of irreversibility.

Exam tips: always ask whether a process is reversible and whether it is adiabatic. Only both together make it isentropic. Compare actual with isentropic states at the same exit pressure.

notes.h: The Rankine cycle and air-standard cycles
notes.body:
A power cycle converts heat into net work continuously. This topic applies the first and second laws to whole plants, using the Carnot cycle as the benchmark.

Why not a Carnot cycle with steam?
- A Carnot cycle inside the wet region would need to compress a wet mixture, which is hard to do, and the turbine would handle very wet steam, which erodes the blades.
- The Rankine cycle fixes both problems. It condenses the steam completely before pumping, and it usually superheats the steam before the turbine.

The ideal Rankine cycle (states 1 to 4)
- 1→2: isentropic pumping of saturated liquid from the condenser pressure to the boiler pressure: w_p = v₁(p₂ − p₁).
- 2→3: constant-pressure heat addition in the boiler and superheater: q_in = h₃ − h₂.
- 3→4: isentropic expansion in the turbine: w_t = h₃ − h₄, with s₄ = s₃.
- 4→1: constant-pressure heat rejection in the condenser: q_out = h₄ − h₁.
- Thermal efficiency: η = (w_t − w_p)/q_in = 1 − q_out/q_in.

Worked example: boiler at 40 bar and 400 °C, condenser at 0.1 bar (approximate IAPWS-IF97 values).
- State 1: h₁ ≈ 191.8 kJ/kg, v₁ ≈ 0.00101 m³/kg.
- Pump: w_p ≈ 0.00101 × (4000 − 10) ≈ 4.0 kJ/kg, so h₂ ≈ 195.8 kJ/kg.
- State 3: h₃ ≈ 3214.4 kJ/kg and s₃ ≈ 6.771 kJ/(kg K).
- State 4: x₄ = (6.771 − 0.649)/7.500 ≈ 0.816, so h₄ ≈ 191.8 + 0.816 × 2392.1 ≈ 2144.5 kJ/kg.
- w_t ≈ 1069.9 kJ/kg and q_in ≈ 3018.6 kJ/kg, so η ≈ (1069.9 − 4.0)/3018.6 ≈ 35.3%.
- The back-work ratio w_p/w_t is only about 0.4%. This is the big advantage of pumping a liquid instead of compressing a gas.
- A Carnot engine between 400 °C and 45.8 °C would reach about 52.6%. The Rankine cycle falls short because most of its heat is added well below the peak temperature.
- With a turbine isentropic efficiency of 0.85, h₄ ≈ 3214.4 − 0.85 × 1069.9 ≈ 2305.0 kJ/kg (x₄ ≈ 0.88) and η falls to about 30.0%.

Improving the Rankine cycle
- Lower the condenser pressure. This lowers the temperature of heat rejection, but makes the turbine exhaust wetter.
- Superheat to a higher temperature. This raises the mean temperature of heat addition and gives drier exhaust.
- Raise the boiler pressure. This raises the mean temperature of heat addition, but makes the exhaust wetter unless reheat is used.
- Reheat and regenerative feed heating are later refinements.

Air-standard gas cycles (cold-air assumptions, γ = 1.4)
- Otto cycle (idealised spark-ignition engine): η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1), where r is the compression ratio. For r = 8, η ≈ 56.5%.
- Joule/Brayton cycle (idealised gas turbine): η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), where r_p is the pressure ratio. For r_p = 10, η ≈ 48.2%.
- These are idealisations, and real engines achieve much lower efficiencies.

Exam tips: tabulate p, T, h, s and x for every state before working out energies, mark the cycle on a T–s diagram, and check that w_net = q_in − q_out.

cards.b: A fixed mass (control mass). Energy can cross the boundary as heat or work, but no mass crosses it. Example: gas in a sealed piston–cylinder.
A region in space with mass flowing in and/or out across its boundary, e.g. a turbine, compressor or nozzle.
Intensive properties do not depend on system size (p, T, density). Extensive properties scale with mass (V, U, H). Extensive ÷ mass = specific property.
Two independent intensive properties fix the state. During a phase change p and T are not independent, so another property such as v or quality is needed.
If bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with body C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is the basis of temperature measurement.
A process slow enough that the system stays infinitesimally close to equilibrium throughout, so its path can be drawn on a property diagram.
Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. Use absolute pressure in pv = RT and in property tables.

cards.f: First law for a closed system
cards.b: Q − W = ΔU (+ΔKE + ΔPE), with Q = heat added to the system and W = work done by the system. Some courses write Q + W = ΔU, counting work done on the system as positive.
W = ∫ p dV: the area under the process path on a p–V diagram. It is zero at constant volume and p(V₂ − V₁) at constant pressure.
W = (p₂V₂ − p₁V₁)/(1 − n) = mR(T₂ − T₁)/(1 − n) for an ideal gas, where pVⁿ = constant.
W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = mRT ln(p₁/p₂). Because ΔU = 0 for an isothermal ideal gas, Q = W.
A quantity such as heat or work that depends on the process path, not only on the end states. Written with δ (δQ, δW) and not a property.
H = U + pV (h = u + pv). For a constant-pressure quasi-static process in a closed system with only boundary work, Q = ΔH.
Δu = c_v ΔT, Δh = c_p ΔT, c_p − c_v = R, γ = c_p/c_v. For air: c_p ≈ 1.005, c_v ≈ 0.718 kJ/(kg K), γ ≈ 1.4.
For pVⁿ = constant with an ideal gas: T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((n−1)/n) = (V₁/V₂)^(n−1).
x = mass of vapour ÷ total mass in a liquid–vapour mixture, 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Any specific property y = y_f + x(y_g − y_f).
Liquid with T below Tsat at its pressure. Approximate its v, u and h by the saturated-liquid values at the same temperature.
Vapour at a temperature above Tsat for its pressure. p and T are independent here, so properties are read from superheat tables at (p, T).
About 374 °C and 220.6 bar (22.06 MPa). Above it there is no distinct liquid–vapour phase change.
Enthalpy of vaporisation: h_g − h_f at a given pressure. It falls as pressure rises and reaches zero at the critical point.

cards.f: Finding phase from p and T
cards.b: Compare T with Tsat(p): below means compressed liquid, above means superheated vapour. If T = Tsat you also need x, v, h or s.
Tsat ≈ 179.9 °C, h_f ≈ 762.5, h_fg ≈ 2014.6, h_g ≈ 2777.1 kJ/kg, v_g ≈ 0.194 m³/kg (IAPWS-IF97; tables may differ slightly).
Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (V₂² − V₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)], with Q̇ = heat added and Ẇ = shaft power produced.
The work needed to push fluid across the control-volume boundary: pv per unit mass. Combined with u it gives enthalpy h = u + pv.
Adiabatic, no work, negligible ΔKE, so h₂ = h₁ (isenthalpic). Pressure drops. It is irreversible, so entropy rises.
V₂ = √(V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂)), with h in J/kg (multiply kJ/kg by 1000). For an ideal gas h₁ − h₂ = c_p(T₁ − T₂).
w_in ≈ v(p₂ − p₁) for an incompressible liquid: small because liquid v is tiny.
ṁ = ρAV = AV/v is the same at every section of a single-stream steady-flow device.
Wet steam is throttled into the superheated region. Measuring p and T there gives h, and since h is unchanged, x = (h − h_f)/h_fg at the upstream pressure.
No device operating in a cycle can receive heat from a single reservoir and produce an equal amount of net work. Every heat engine must reject some heat.
No device operating in a cycle can have as its sole effect the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter body.
η = 1 − T_L/T_H (temperatures in kelvin): the maximum efficiency of any heat engine operating between reservoirs at T_H and T_L.

cards.f: Maximum COP of a heat pump
cards.b: COP_HP = T_H/(T_H − T_L) in kelvin. For a refrigerator, COP_R = T_L/(T_H − T_L). Note COP_HP = COP_R + 1.
(1) No engine is more efficient than a reversible one between the same two reservoirs. (2) All reversible engines between the same reservoirs have equal efficiency, whatever the working fluid.
Friction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, free (unrestrained) expansion, mixing, electrical resistance and inelastic deformation.
Reversible isothermal heat addition, reversible adiabatic expansion, reversible isothermal heat rejection, reversible adiabatic compression.
∮δQ/T ≤ 0 for any cycle, with equality only for a reversible cycle.
S₂ − S₁ = ∫δQ/T + S_gen, where S_gen ≥ 0 and S_gen = 0 only for reversible processes.
A process at constant entropy: adiabatic and reversible together. Adiabatic alone is not enough.
Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁) (constant specific heats).
η_T = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s): actual work ÷ ideal isentropic work to the same exit pressure.
η_C = (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁): ideal isentropic work ÷ actual work to the same exit pressure.
T ds = du + p dv and T ds = dh − v dp. They relate properties, so they hold for any process between equilibrium states.
For an isolated system (or system plus surroundings), ΔS_total = S_gen ≥ 0.
1→2 isentropic pump; 2→3 constant-p heat addition (boiler/superheater); 3→4 isentropic turbine expansion; 4→1 constant-p condensation to saturated liquid.
η = (w_t − w_p)/q_in = [(h₃ − h₄) − (h₂ − h₁)]/(h₃ − h₂).
Pump (or compressor) work ÷ turbine work. Tiny for a Rankine cycle (liquid pumped) and large for a gas turbine (gas compressed).

cards.f: Why superheat in a Rankine cycle?
cards.b: It raises the mean temperature of heat addition, which increases efficiency, and gives drier turbine exhaust, which reduces blade erosion.
η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1), r = compression ratio (cold-air standard). For r = 8 and γ = 1.4, η ≈ 56.5%.
η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), r_p = pressure ratio (cold-air standard). For r_p = 10, η ≈ 48.2%.
It lowers the heat-rejection temperature, so efficiency rises, but turbine exhaust quality falls (wetter steam).

questions.q: Which of these is an intensive property?
questions.why: Temperature does not change if you split the system into two halves, so it is intensive. Volume, mass and internal energy all halve when the system is halved, so they are extensive. Internal energy only becomes intensive when expressed per unit mass (specific internal energy u).

questions.q: A 0.5 m³ rigid tank holds air (R = 287 J/(kg K)) at 5 bar and 27 °C. What is the mass of air?
questions.why: m = pV/(RT) = (5 × 10⁵ × 0.5)/(287 × 300.15) ≈ 2.90 kg. Using 27 instead of 300.15 for the temperature (Celsius, not kelvin) gives 32.3 kg. Entering pressure as 500 kPa while keeping R in J/(kg K) is a factor of 1000 out and gives 0.00290 kg. Using the universal constant 8.314 J/(mol K) in place of R gives about 100, but that is the amount in moles, not a mass in kilograms.

questions.q: Distinguish between a closed system and a control volume, giving one engineering example of each. State the state postulate and explain why pressure and temperature alone cannot fix the state of wet steam.
markScheme: Closed system: fixed mass, energy (heat/work) crosses boundary, no mass transfer; example given (1)
Control volume: mass crosses boundary; example such as turbine, pump or nozzle (1)
State postulate: two independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible pure substance (1)
In the two-phase region p and T are linked (T = Tsat(p)), so they are not independent; need quality or v, u, h, s (1)
questions.modelAnswer: A closed system is a fixed quantity of matter. Heat and work can cross its boundary but mass cannot; air compressed in a sealed piston–cylinder is an example. A control volume is a region of space through which mass flows, such as a steam turbine, where steam enters and leaves continuously. The state postulate says that the state of a simple compressible pure substance is fixed by two independent intensive properties. For wet steam, the temperature is always the saturation temperature at the given pressure, so knowing p tells you T and the two are not independent. A second independent property, usually the dryness fraction x (or v, h or s), is needed to fix the state.

questions.q: A rigid sealed tank of gas receives 50 kJ of heat. There is no stirrer or electrical input. Taking Q as heat added and W as work done by the gas, which statement is correct?
questions.why: A rigid boundary cannot move, so the boundary work is zero, and Q − W = ΔU gives ΔU = +50 kJ. Saying W = 50 kJ with ΔU = 0 wrongly assumes the heat leaves as work, which is impossible with no moving boundary or shaft. ΔU = −50 kJ comes from treating heat supplied as negative. ΔU = +50 kJ together with W = +50 kJ breaks the first law, because 50 − 50 would make ΔU zero.

questions.q: Air at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed quasi-statically following pV¹·³ = constant to 8 bar. What is the final temperature?
questions.why: T₂ = T₁(p₂/p₁)^((n−1)/n) = 300 × 8^(0.3/1.3) ≈ 485 K. Using γ = 1.4 in place of n = 1.3 gives the isentropic result of about 543 K. Writing T₂ = T₁ × p₂/p₁ = 2400 K treats the process as constant volume, ignoring the reduction in volume. 300 K would only be correct for an isothermal process (n = 1).

questions.q: 0.1 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K), c_v = 0.718 kJ/(kg K)) at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed quasi-statically following pV¹·³ = constant to 8 bar. Find the final temperature, the work done and the heat transfer, stating your sign convention.
markScheme: Q = ΔU + W ≈ 13.3 − 17.7 = −4.4 kJ: heat rejected, with convention stated (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Convention: Q is heat added to the air and W is work done by the air, so Q − W = ΔU. Temperature: T₂ = 300 × 8^(0.3/1.3) = 300 × 1.616 ≈ 484.8 K. Work: W = mR(T₂ − T₁)/(1 − n) = 0.1 × 0.287 × 184.8/(1 − 1.3) ≈ −17.7 kJ, so 17.7 kJ of work is done on the air. Internal energy: ΔU = 0.1 × 0.718 × 184.8 ≈ 13.3 kJ. Heat: Q = ΔU + W = 13.3 + (−17.7) ≈ −4.4 kJ, so about 4.4 kJ of heat leaves the air during the compression.

questions.q: Water is at 10 bar and 150 °C. Given Tsat(10 bar) ≈ 179.9 °C, what is its phase?
questions.why: The temperature is below the saturation temperature at 10 bar, so the water has not started to boil: it is a compressed liquid. Calling it superheated comes from comparing 150 °C with the 100 °C boiling point at atmospheric pressure instead of with Tsat at 10 bar. A wet mixture is only possible when T equals Tsat. Supercritical would need a pressure above about 220.6 bar.

questions.q: Wet steam at 1 bar has h = 1546 kJ/kg. Using h_f ≈ 417.5, h_fg ≈ 2257.5 and h_g ≈ 2675.0 kJ/kg, what is its dryness fraction?
questions.why: x = (h − h_f)/h_fg = (1546 − 417.5)/2257.5 ≈ 0.50. Dividing h by h_g (1546/2675) gives 0.58, which ignores the liquid's enthalpy. Dividing h by h_fg without first subtracting h_f gives 0.68. Subtracting h_f but then dividing by h_g instead of h_fg gives 0.42.

questions.q: Steam at 10 bar has a dryness fraction of 0.9. Using v_f ≈ 0.00113 m³/kg, v_g ≈ 0.1944 m³/kg, h_f ≈ 762.5 kJ/kg and h_fg ≈ 2014.6 kJ/kg, find its temperature, specific volume and specific enthalpy, and the volume occupied by 2 kg.
questions.modelAnswer: The steam is wet, so it is at the saturation temperature for 10 bar, about 179.9 °C. Specific volume: v = v_f + x(v_g − v_f) = 0.00113 + 0.9 × (0.1944 − 0.00113) ≈ 0.175 m³/kg. Enthalpy: h = h_f + x h_fg = 762.5 + 0.9 × 2014.6 ≈ 2575.6 kJ/kg. Volume of 2 kg: V = 2 × 0.175 ≈ 0.350 m³. These values are approximate (based on IAPWS-IF97) and your data book may differ in the last figure.

questions.q: Air (c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg K)) enters an adiabatic nozzle with negligible velocity and cools from 500 K to 440 K. What is the exit velocity?
questions.why: V₂ = √(2c_pΔT) = √(2 × 1005 × 60) ≈ 347 m/s. Leaving c_p in kJ/(kg K) gives √(2 × 1.005 × 60) ≈ 11 m/s, because V²/2 must be in J/kg. Forgetting the factor of 2 in V²/2 gives √(1005 × 60) ≈ 246 m/s. Using c_v (718 J/(kg K)) gives about 294 m/s, but the enthalpy change in a flow device uses c_p.

questions.q: Which property stays constant across an adiabatic throttling valve with negligible change in kinetic energy?
questions.why: With no heat, no work and negligible ΔKE and ΔPE, the SFEE reduces to h₂ = h₁. Entropy is not constant: throttling is highly irreversible, so entropy rises, and assuming otherwise mixes up adiabatic with isentropic. Temperature is constant only for an ideal gas, whose h depends on T alone; steam and refrigerants usually cool. Pressure is the property the valve is designed to reduce.

questions.q: Steam flows steadily through an adiabatic turbine at 10 kg/s. It enters at 30 bar and 350 °C (h ≈ 3116.1 kJ/kg) and leaves at 0.1 bar with dryness fraction 0.9 (h_f ≈ 191.8, h_fg ≈ 2392.1 kJ/kg). Neglecting changes in kinetic and potential energy, find the power output. State your assumptions.
markScheme: Assumptions: steady flow, adiabatic, ΔKE and ΔPE negligible (1)
SFEE reduces to Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂) (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Assume steady flow, an adiabatic turbine and negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy. The SFEE becomes Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂). The exit state is wet, so h₂ = h_f + x h_fg = 191.8 + 0.9 × 2392.1 ≈ 2344.7 kJ/kg. Specific work: w = 3116.1 − 2344.7 ≈ 771.4 kJ/kg. Power: Ẇ = 10 × 771.4 ≈ 7714 kW ≈ 7.71 MW.

questions.q: What is the maximum possible thermal efficiency of a heat engine working between reservoirs at 527 °C and 27 °C?
options: It depends on the working fluid
questions.why: In kelvin the reservoirs are 800 K and 300 K, so η = 1 − 300/800 = 62.5%. Using Celsius temperatures (1 − 27/527) gives 94.9%. Working out T_L/T_H (300/800) instead of 1 − T_L/T_H gives 37.5%, which is the fraction of heat rejected. The Carnot principles say every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same efficiency, so the working fluid does not matter.

questions.q: What is the highest COP a heat pump can have when keeping a room at 20 °C with outside air at 0 °C?
questions.why: COP_HP = T_H/(T_H − T_L) = 293.15/20 ≈ 14.7. The value 13.7 is T_L/(T_H − T_L), which is the refrigerator COP: the heat delivered to the room also includes the work input. About 0.068 is the inverse of the heat-pump COP. 1.0 comes from using Celsius, 20/(20 − 0).

questions.q: An inventor claims an engine that receives 600 kW of heat from a source at 800 K, rejects heat to surroundings at 300 K and produces 400 kW of net work. Assess the claim using the second law, and state the minimum rate of heat rejection for an engine with this heat input.
markScheme: Claim exceeds the reversible limit, so it violates the second law (Carnot principle / Kelvin–Planck) and is impossible (1)
questions.modelAnswer: The claimed efficiency is 400/600 ≈ 66.7%. No engine can be more efficient than a reversible engine between the same two reservoirs, and that limit is η = 1 − T_L/T_H = 1 − 300/800 = 62.5%. The claim exceeds this, so it breaks the second law and must be rejected. With 600 kW of heat input, the most work any engine could produce is 0.625 × 600 = 375 kW. The least heat it could reject is therefore 600 − 375 = 225 kW, whereas the claimed engine would reject only 200 kW.

questions.q: 1000 kJ of heat flows directly from a reservoir at 500 K to a reservoir at 300 K. How much entropy is generated?
questions.why: The hot reservoir loses 1000/500 = 2 kJ/K and the cold one gains 1000/300 ≈ 3.33 kJ/K, so S_gen ≈ 1.33 kJ/K. Zero would mean the heat transfer is reversible, but heat moving across a finite temperature difference is irreversible. Adding the two magnitudes (2 + 3.33) ignores the fact that the hot reservoir loses entropy, giving 5.33 kJ/K. Q/ΔT = 1000/200 = 5 kJ/K is not an entropy formula.

questions.q: Which statement about an adiabatic process in a closed system is always true?
options: The entropy of the system cannot decrease
The entropy of the system stays constant
The entropy can fall if work is done on the system
The entropy changes only if the temperature changes
questions.why: With δQ = 0 the entropy balance gives ΔS = S_gen ≥ 0, so entropy cannot fall. Constant entropy holds only if the process is also reversible; assuming it always does mixes up adiabatic with isentropic. Work carries no entropy across the boundary, so doing work on the system cannot reduce its entropy. Entropy can rise at constant temperature, for example in the free expansion of an ideal gas.

questions.q: Air (c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K), γ = 1.4) at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed adiabatically to 8 bar. The isentropic efficiency is 0.85. Find the exit temperature, the specific work input and the specific entropy change, and comment on its sign.
markScheme: Positive because the process is adiabatic but irreversible: Δs = s_gen > 0 (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Isentropic exit temperature: T₂s = 300 × 8^(0.2857) ≈ 543.4 K. From η_C = (T₂s − T₁)/(T₂ − T₁), the actual exit temperature is T₂ = 300 + (543.4 − 300)/0.85 ≈ 586.4 K. Work input (SFEE, adiabatic, ΔKE negligible): w = c_p(T₂ − T₁) = 1.005 × 286.4 ≈ 287.8 kJ/kg, compared with about 244.7 kJ/kg if the compression were isentropic. Entropy change: Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) = 1.005 ln(1.9546) − 0.287 ln 8 ≈ 0.6735 − 0.5968 ≈ 0.077 kJ/(kg K). No heat crosses the boundary, so this rise is all entropy generated by irreversibility (friction and turbulence), which the second law requires to be positive.

questions.q: In an ideal Rankine cycle h₁ = 191.8, h₂ = 195.8, h₃ = 3214.4 and h₄ = 2144.5 kJ/kg, where 1 is the pump inlet and 3 the turbine inlet. What is the thermal efficiency?
questions.why: η = [(h₃ − h₄) − (h₂ − h₁)]/(h₃ − h₂) = (1069.9 − 4.0)/3018.6 ≈ 35.3%. Dividing the turbine work by h₃ instead of by the heat added (h₃ − h₂) gives 33.3%. The value 64.7% is q_out/q_in = (h₄ − h₁)/(h₃ − h₂), the fraction of heat rejected, which equals 1 − η. 52.6% is the Carnot efficiency between 400 °C and 45.8 °C, which a Rankine cycle cannot reach.

questions.q: What is the cold-air-standard efficiency of an Otto cycle with compression ratio 8 (γ = 1.4)?
questions.why: η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1) = 1 − 8^(−0.4) ≈ 56.5%. Leaving out the exponent (1 − 1/8) gives 87.5%. Using the Joule-cycle form with exponent (γ − 1)/γ and treating 8 as a pressure ratio gives about 44.8%. The value 43.5% is 8^(−0.4) alone, which forgets to subtract from 1.

questions.q: A Rankine cycle has steam entering the turbine at 40 bar and 400 °C (h ≈ 3214.4 kJ/kg) and a condenser at 0.1 bar. Isentropic expansion would give h₄s ≈ 2144.5 kJ/kg. The feed pump adds 4.0 kJ/kg, giving h₂ ≈ 195.8 kJ/kg. The turbine isentropic efficiency is 0.85. Find the actual turbine exit enthalpy and dryness fraction (h_f ≈ 191.8, h_fg ≈ 2392.1 kJ/kg at 0.1 bar), and the cycle efficiency.
markScheme: Comment: η falls from about 35.3% (ideal) to about 30.0%, and the exhaust is drier than in the isentropic case (x ≈ 0.88 vs 0.82) (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Isentropic turbine work = 3214.4 − 2144.5 = 1069.9 kJ/kg, so the actual work is 0.85 × 1069.9 ≈ 909.4 kJ/kg. The actual exit enthalpy is h₄ = 3214.4 − 909.4 ≈ 2305.0 kJ/kg. At 0.1 bar this gives x₄ = (2305.0 − 191.8)/2392.1 ≈ 0.883. Heat input: q_in = 3214.4 − 195.8 = 3018.6 kJ/kg. Efficiency: η = (909.4 − 4.0)/3018.6 ≈ 0.300, or about 30.0%, compared with about 35.3% for the ideal cycle. Note that the irreversible expansion leaves the exhaust drier (x ≈ 0.88) than the isentropic case (x ≈ 0.82), because some of the work lost to friction stays in the steam as enthalpy.

questions.q:
A steam power plant runs on a simple Rankine cycle. Steam leaves the boiler at 40 bar and 400 °C, and the condenser pressure is 0.1 bar. The net power output is 50 MW. Use these approximate property values: at 0.1 bar, Tsat ≈ 45.8 °C, v_f ≈ 0.00101 m³/kg, h_f ≈ 191.8 kJ/kg, h_fg ≈ 2392.1 kJ/kg, s_f ≈ 0.649 kJ/(kg K), s_fg ≈ 7.500 kJ/(kg K); at 40 bar and 400 °C, h ≈ 3214.4 kJ/kg, s ≈ 6.771 kJ/(kg K).
(a) Sketch the cycle on a T–s diagram, marking the saturation dome and states 1–4. [3]
(b) Find the pump work per kg. [3]
(c) Assuming isentropic expansion, find the turbine exit dryness fraction and the turbine work per kg. [5]
(d) Find the thermal efficiency and the steam mass flow rate. [5]
(e) Compare the efficiency with that of a Carnot engine between the same maximum and minimum temperatures, and explain the difference. [4]
markScheme: (a) T–s sketch: pump line nearly vertical in liquid region, constant-pressure heating into superheat, vertical expansion into wet region, horizontal condensation line (3)
(e) Rankine lower because much heat is added at lower temperatures (feed-water heating, evaporation at 250 °C), so the mean temperature of heat addition is well below 400 °C (2)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) On the T–s diagram, state 1 is saturated liquid at 0.1 bar (45.8 °C) on the left of the dome. The pump (1→2) is a short vertical line to 40 bar in the compressed-liquid region. Heat addition (2→3) follows the 40 bar constant-pressure line: it heats the liquid up to about 250 °C, crosses the dome horizontally during boiling, then rises into the superheat region to 400 °C. The turbine expansion (3→4) is a vertical line down into the wet region at 45.8 °C. Condensation (4→1) is a horizontal line back to state 1.

(b) Pump work: w_p = v₁(p₂ − p₁) = 0.00101 × (4000 − 10) kPa ≈ 4.03 kJ/kg, so h₂ = 191.8 + 4.0 ≈ 195.8 kJ/kg.

(c) Isentropic expansion means s₄ = s₃ = 6.771 kJ/(kg K). Then x₄ = (s₄ − s_f)/s_fg = (6.771 − 0.649)/7.500 ≈ 0.816. The exit enthalpy is h₄ = 191.8 + 0.816 × 2392.1 ≈ 2144.5 kJ/kg, so the turbine work is w_t = 3214.4 − 2144.5 ≈ 1069.9 kJ/kg.

(d) Heat input: q_in = h₃ − h₂ = 3214.4 − 195.8 = 3018.6 kJ/kg. Net work: w_net = 1069.9 − 4.0 = 1065.9 kJ/kg. Efficiency: η = 1065.9/3018.6 ≈ 0.353, or about 35.3%. Mass flow: ṁ = 50 000 kW / 1065.9 kJ/kg ≈ 46.9 kg/s. Check: q_out = h₄ − h₁ ≈ 1952.7 kJ/kg, and q_in − q_out ≈ 1065.9 kJ/kg, which agrees.

(e) The maximum temperature is 673.15 K and the minimum is 318.96 K, so the Carnot efficiency is 1 − 318.96/673.15 ≈ 52.6%. The Rankine cycle rejects all its heat at the minimum temperature, as a Carnot cycle does. However, it adds a large share of its heat while warming the feed water from about 46 °C and boiling it at about 250 °C, well below 400 °C. Its mean temperature of heat addition is therefore much lower than T_max, which reduces efficiency. The cycle is still preferred in practice because pumping a liquid needs very little work and the turbine does not have to handle very wet steam over its whole expansion. (All property values are approximate, from IAPWS-IF97.)

questions.q:
Air (treat as an ideal gas with c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K), γ = 1.4) flows steadily at 2 kg/s through an adiabatic compressor. It enters at 1 bar and 300 K and leaves at 8 bar. The isentropic efficiency is 0.85. Changes in kinetic and potential energy are negligible.
(a) Find the isentropic and actual exit temperatures. [4]
(b) Find the power input. [3]
(c) Find the rate of entropy generation in the compressor, and explain how it is consistent with the second law. [5]
(d) The compressed air is then cooled at constant pressure back to 300 K by surroundings at 300 K. Find the heat rejected per kg and the entropy generated per kg in the cooling process. [5]
(e) Explain why the power needed would fall if the compression were split into two stages with intercooling. [3]
markScheme: (c) Positive because adiabatic and irreversible; zero only if isentropic (1)
(e) Intercooling lowers the temperature (and specific volume) entering the second stage; work ∫v dp is smaller; approaches isothermal compression (3)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Isentropic exit temperature: T₂s = T₁(p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) = 300 × 8^0.2857 ≈ 543.4 K. From η_C = (T₂s − T₁)/(T₂ − T₁), the actual exit temperature is T₂ = 300 + (543.4 − 300)/0.85 ≈ 586.4 K.

(b) The SFEE for an adiabatic compressor with negligible ΔKE and ΔPE gives Ẇ_in = ṁc_p(T₂ − T₁) = 2 × 1.005 × 286.4 ≈ 575.7 kW, or about 576 kW.

(c) Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) = 1.005 ln(1.9546) − 0.287 ln 8 = 0.6735 − 0.5968 ≈ 0.0768 kJ/(kg K). The compressor is adiabatic, so no entropy is carried in or out with heat, and in steady flow Ṡ_gen = ṁ(s₂ − s₁) ≈ 2 × 0.0768 ≈ 0.154 kW/K. This is positive, as the second law requires for an irreversible process. It would be zero only for the isentropic compressor, for which Δs = 0 (with these constants, 1.005 ln(543.4/300) − 0.287 ln 8 is zero to rounding).

(d) Heat rejected: q = c_p(T₂ − 300) = 1.005 × 286.4 ≈ 287.8 kJ/kg. The pressure is constant, so the entropy change of the air is Δs_air = c_p ln(300/586.4) ≈ −0.674 kJ/(kg K). The surroundings receive 287.8 kJ/kg at 300 K, so Δs_surr = 287.8/300 ≈ 0.959 kJ/(kg K). Entropy generated: s_gen = −0.674 + 0.959 ≈ 0.286 kJ/(kg K). This is positive because the heat crosses a finite temperature difference: the air starts at 586 K, while the surroundings are at 300 K.

(e) In steady flow, the reversible work per kg is ∫v dp. Gas at a lower temperature has a smaller specific volume, so it needs less work to compress through the same pressure rise. Cooling the air between stages brings it back towards 300 K before the second stage, so the overall process gets closer to isothermal compression, which needs the least work. The saving is the area between the single-stage and two-stage paths on a p–v diagram.
